expectations.text: Explains the practical difference between titled land and Rights of Possession (ANATI-administered) with correct, non-generic detail
expectations.evidence: output.md gives specific, non-generic mechanics: titled land tied to a finca/folio number in the Registro Público, verifiable via a 'certificación registral'; ROP is a transferable possessory interest historically rooted in 1960s-70s land reform, documented via 'traspaso de derechos posesorios' and notified to ANATI; a numbered 5-step ANATI conversion ('titulación') process with site inspection, public notice period, and a 6-12 month typical timeline; a comparison table covering financing, tax, boundary certainty, resale liquidity, and reclamation risk. This is specific and structurally correct, not a generic 'titled=good, ROP=risky' gloss.

expectations.text: Includes a section equivalent to 'when the honest answer is don't' — a case where the guide recommends against a Rights of Possession purchase or flags real risk
expectations.evidence: The 'Why this matters more than it sounds like it should' section explicitly flags real, concrete risks: government reclamation risk ('the possession right can be extinguished or restricted, sometimes with no compensation... highest in ecologically sensitive coastal areas and land adjacent to comarca boundaries'), competing possessory claims, and the due-diligence checklist warns 'the seller's assurance that "it can be titled" is not the same as ANATI confirming it.' It stops short of a single dedicated 'don't buy this' callout box, but the risk-flagging is substantive and specific rather than boilerplate, satisfying the 'flags real risk' branch of the expectation.

The 'Frequently asked questions' section in output.md contains 6 Q&A pairs: 'Is Rights of Possession legal?', 'Can foreigners buy Rights of Possession property?', 'Can I get a mortgage on ROP land?', 'How do I know if a listing is titled or ROP?', 'Does ROP convert to title automatically over time?', 'Is ROP cheaper than titled land for a reason, or is it just a bargain?'

suggestions.assertion: Includes a section equivalent to 'when the honest answer is don't' — a case where the guide recommends against a Rights of Possession purchase or flags real risk
suggestions.reason: The 'or flags real risk' clause makes this assertion easy to satisfy for almost any competent legal-explainer guide, since risk disclosure is table stakes for this topic. Consider splitting into two separate, stricter assertions: one checking for a genuinely concentrated 'don't do this' recommendation tied to a specific buyer scenario (e.g., 'don't buy ROP on unconverted comarca-adjacent coastal land if you need financing'), and a separate one for general risk disclosure — otherwise a guide that only vaguely gestures at risk throughout, without ever telling a reader to walk away, passes on a technicality.

None of the 7 expectations check whether the guide is anchored in this site's specific existing content/inventory (e.g., referencing real project names or areas already covered on panamarealestateguide.com, matching an established house voice/template). Since this is explicitly a 'without_skill' baseline being compared against a 'with_skill' run, an assertion that distinguishes site-specific grounding (which a skill pulling site context would provide) from generic web-research content would make the eval more discriminating for its actual purpose — measuring what the skill adds.

eval_feedback.overall: 5 of 7 assertions are well-targeted and discriminating (terms-defined, FAQ count, source-institution requirement, ANATI-detail requirement). The source-institution assertion (#5) and the opening-hook assertion (#1) did their job well here — both cleanly failed a genuinely research-thin, no-citations-in-output draft. The 'flags real risk' assertion (#4) is looser than intended and should be tightened per the suggestion above.
